p: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.

notes: The article says Debi Chand (1720-6) 'was defeated by the British troops' in the Rohilla wars; that looks wrong for the 1720s and I left it out.
The article gives 685 CE (1849 report) and 700 CE (Pandey) as traditional dates for Som Chand; I used only the first.
The existing description says Kalyan Chand moved the capital 'around 1563'; the article says 1563 flatly. Not repeated.
